analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $9.80 over two years, then indexes it to inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the minimum wage from $7.25 to $9.80 an hour was introduced in July 2012 with 17 Senate backers, referred to committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage in steps: to $8.10 an hour a few months after passage, $8.95 after one year, and $9.80 after two years [S2] [S3]. After that, the wage would rise automatically each year with the cost of living, so it would not erode again as it did between 2009 and this bill [S2] [S3]. It would also raise the separate minimum cash wage for tipped workers, such as waiters, to $3.00 an hour and then step it up until it reached 70% of the full minimum wage, ending the long freeze of that $2.13 figure [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum — heavily concentrated in restaurants, retail, hotels, and caregiving — would see their pay rise in steps to $9.80 an hour, and tipped workers would see their base cash wage rise from $2.13 toward 70% of the full minimum. Millions of workers whose pay is pegged just above the minimum would also likely get a lift. The automatic inflation index would keep the wage from losing value in future years without Congress having to act again.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $8.10, then $8.95, then $9.80 an hour over roughly two years.
After two years, adjusts the minimum wage annually for inflation using the Consumer Price Index, so its purchasing power no longer depends on future acts of Congress.
Raises the minimum cash wage for tipped employees to $3.00 an hour in the first year, then by up to $0.85 a year until it reaches 70% of the full minimum wage.
Requires the Labor Department to publish each upcoming increase 60 days in advance in the Federal Register and on its website, giving employers and workers notice.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that employ large numbers of minimum-wage and tipped workers — restaurants, retail stores, hotels, and other low-wage service employers — would bear higher payroll costs, and would likely pass some of that on through prices or reduced hours. The Restaurant Association and other employer groups opposed similar proposals, though the record here shows no floor debate because the bill never got that far.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retail, and other low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: Employers of minimum-wage and tipped workers — especially restaurants and small food-service businesses — would face immediately higher payroll costs, phased in over two years, and would likely offset some of it through higher menu prices, tighter staffing, or reduced hours.

The tipped-wage formula raises the base cash wage for tipped employees to $3.00 only in year one and then steps it up gradually, so tipped workers would spend years below 70% of the full minimum before reaching it.
A higher wage floor applies nationwide, despite wide differences in living costs and prevailing wages across states; in low-wage regions it represents a larger shock than in high-wage cities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers covered, the gains are direct and substantial: roughly a 35% raise in the minimum wage over two years, plus an end to the erosion of its value and the first increase in the tipped base wage since 1991. The costs fall on a concentrated set of employers in the restaurant and retail sectors, spread in part across consumers through modest price increases. The main honest objection is the national one-size-fits-all level and the strain on small food-service businesses; the design mitigates this with a phase-in, advance notice, and automatic rather than abrupt jumps. On balance the benefits to low-wage workers outweigh the costs, which is a large part of why it never reached a vote: opponents preferred the status quo.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee in July 2012, and that is where it stayed: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the bill on July 26, 2012, joined by 15 Democratic and 1 Independent cosponsor.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced.
The action history records no further steps — no committee markup, no committee report, no floor vote — and the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 without the bill ever coming up.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low-wage employers — restaurants, retail chains, and other businesses paying the $7.25 minimum — are better off, since wages stayed where they were. Workers earning the minimum gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.role: Senator from Iowa; bill sponsor; Chairman, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Minimum Wage Act of 2012 and recruited 16 cosponsors; as chairman of the committee to which it was referred, never scheduled it for a markup or vote.

for.name: 16 Senate cosponsors (15 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction, including Mikulski, Murray, Sanders, Merkley, Durbin, Schumer, and Gillibrand.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee (112th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral on July 26, 2012; took no recorded action — no hearing or markup — for the remaining five months of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican majority (112th Congress)
against.role: Controlled the House chamber and its floor schedule
against.what_they_did: No House action was ever taken; had the Senate passed the bill, the Republican-run House had shown no interest in minimum-wage legislation and was not expected to bring it to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill died in a Senate committee without a recorded vote, so no roll-call splits it, but the sponsorship pattern was entirely along party lines.

industries.note: The largest employer of tipped workers, whose base cash wage would rise from $2.13 to $3.00 and beyond, on top of higher wages for all staff. The industry's interest in keeping the current wage floor runs directly against the pay of the workers it employs.

industries.industry: Retail and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: Would face higher payroll costs under the step-up to $9.80 an hour. Their savings from the current $7.25 floor are money not paid to the workers serving them.
The direct beneficiaries: a phased raise to $9.80, annual inflation adjustments, and a rising base wage for tipped employees.
